content.title: Why v² and not v
content.body:
Distance is speed times time, but with braking neither factor is fixed. Braking takes longer at higher speed AND the average speed during that time is higher. Both effects scale with v, so distance scales with v times v, i.e. v².

Energy view: kinetic energy is \frac{1}{2}mv^2. The brakes must remove all of it, and the maximum rate they can remove it (force times distance, or power) is fixed by friction, so d = v²/(2a). Double v, quadruple d.

content.title: Common trap
content.body: The square applies only to the braking part where deceleration is constant. Thinking distance is v times reaction time, so it really is proportional to v. Total stopping distance is not purely quadratic; only the braking term is. Also note a = mu g, so doubling mu halves d, while doubling v multiplies d by four.

blocks.title: Three compartments, three jobs
blocks.body: Location separates the stages. Glycolysis sits in the cytosol, needs no membrane and no oxygen, and nets a small ATP return plus reduced NAD. operations.title: Where each stage happens and what it delivers

blocks.title: Locations and net outputs
blocks.body:
Glycolysis: cytosol. One glucose becomes two pyruvate; net gain 2 ATP (4 made, 2 used) and 2 reduced NAD. No oxygen needed.

Link reaction and Krebs cycle: mitochondrial matrix. Pyruvate is decarboxylated and dehydrogenated; carbon leaves as CO2 and carriers are loaded with reduced NAD and FAD. No ATP from the Krebs cycle directly, only a little GTP (counts as ATP).

Oxidative phosphorylation: inner mitochondrial membrane. Reduced carriers release electrons to the electron transport chain; the energy pumps protons, and the gradient drives ATP synthase. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor, forming water.

content.title: Why the ATP number varies
content.body: Two separate losses explain the range, and they act at different points. First, the proton gradient is not spent only on ATP synthase: some protons leak back across the inner mitochondrial membrane through other routes, so not every proton pumped drives ATP synthesis. Second, the reduced NAD made in the cytosol during glycolysis cannot cross the inner mitochondrial membrane directly, so its electrons are shuttled in by carrier molecules. The glycerol phosphate shuttle transfers them to FAD inside the mitochondrion, which feeds the chain further down; the malate aspartate shuttle transfers them to mitochondrial NAD. Because FAD enters at a lower point, it pumps fewer protons and yields less ATP, so which shuttle a tissue uses changes the total. This is why the figure is quoted as a range with stated assumptions, not a fixed constant.

content.title: How the stages link up
content.body: The three stages form a relay rather than three independent reactions. Glycolysis in the cytosol supplies pyruvate and reduced NAD. The link reaction and Krebs cycle in the matrix oxidise the carbon fully, releasing carbon dioxide and loading reduced NAD and FAD. Oxidative phosphorylation uses those reduced carriers: electrons pass down the chain to oxygen as the final electron acceptor, and the proton gradient that is built drives ATP synthase. So the overall equation is a summary of the whole relay, and it shows only the net inputs and outputs, not the carriers or the ATP actually produced.

blocks.title: From the equation to buffer behaviour
blocks.body: The equation pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]) separates two ideas. The pKa fixes roughly where the buffer works; the ratio [A-]/[HA] fine-tunes pH. Equal concentrations give a ratio of 1, log(1) = 0, so pH = pKa. That is the point of maximum buffering. A tenfold excess of base form adds 1 pH unit; a tenfold excess of acid form subtracts 1. This is the same base-ten logic that makes one pH unit a tenfold change in hydrogen ion concentration.

blocks.title: Rearranged for the ratio
blocks.explanation: Useful when a target pH is given and the required ratio of the two forms must be found.

blocks.title: What each component does on adding acid or base

blocks.prompt: A buffer has pKa 6.8. What is its pH when [A-] is ten times [HA]?
blocks.rationale: log(10) = 1, so pH = pKa + 1 = 6.8 + 1 = 7.8. Option 5.8 would be the result if the acid form were ten times the base form.

blocks.title: Closest to pKa, strongest resistance
blocks.body: Buffer capacity is largest when pH is within about one unit of pKa, i.e. when the ratio [A-]/[HA] lies between 0.1 and 10. Outside that band one form dominates and the solution resists pH change poorly.

blocks.title: What each term means
blocks.body: HA is the weak acid form (the proton donor), A⁻ is its conjugate base. pKa is the pH at which the two forms are equally abundant, so it sets the centre of the buffering range. The log term is the ratio of base to acid: it shifts pH up when base dominates and down when acid dominates.

blocks.title: Henderson–Hasselbalch
blocks.explanation: Taking -log10 of the acid dissociation expression K_a = [H+][A-]/[HA] and rearranging gives this form. It is an approximation: it ignores activity coefficients and assumes the acid is weak enough that [HA] at equilibrium is close to the amount added.

content.title: When acid and base are equal
content.body: If [HA] = [A^-], the fraction in the log term equals 1, and log_10 1 = 0. So pH = pK_a. This is the point where the buffer resists pH change best, because both mopping-up forms are equally available. Note: equal amounts means equal concentrations (or moles in the same volume), not equal masses — a weak acid and its conjugate base usually have different molar masses.

content.title: Away from equal amounts
content.body: The ratio is what matters, not either concentration alone. A 10:1 ratio gives log_10 10 = 1, so pH = pK_a + 1 for [A^-]/[HA] = 10, and pH = pK_a - 1 for the reverse 1:10. Useful buffer range is roughly pK_a ± 1, i.e. ratios from about 1:10 to 10:1.

blocks.title: What the determinant measures
blocks.body: Take the unit square spanned by the basis vectors. Its image under the map is the parallelogram spanned by the columns of the matrix. The determinant is the area of that parallelogram: it reports the factor by which the map rescales every area, not just this one.

blocks.title: Signed area of the image parallelogram
blocks.latex: \det\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix} = ad - bc
blocks.explanation: The columns (a, c) and (b, d) span the image of the unit square. A signed area is needed because the bare area ad - bc can go negative.

blocks.title: Why the sign matters
blocks.body: A negative determinant means orientation was reversed: a counterclockwise turn becomes clockwise. The magnitude is the area factor. A determinant of zero collapses the parallelogram to a segment or a point, so distinct inputs share an output and no inverse can exist.

nodes.label: Sign of ad - bc gives orientation

The map has no inverse.

blocks.rationale: The magnitude 3 is the area scaling factor, so areas are multiplied by 3. The negative sign means orientation is flipped. Zero would be the value that rules out an inverse, not -3.

content.title: Why the columns are the images
content.body: Write the input as v = x e1 + y e2, where e1 and e2 are the basis vectors. Linearity gives T(v) = x T(e1) + y T(e2). So the output depends on e1, e2 only through T(e1) and T(e2): their coordinates become the columns of the matrix. Multiplying the matrix by the coordinate column (x, y) then rebuilds x T(e1) + y T(e2). Confusion to avoid: the rows are not the images of the basis vectors, and the entries are not where the basis vectors end up unless the output basis is the standard one.

content.title: Why ad - bc = 0 blocks inversion
content.body: The columns are T(e1) and T(e2). If their determinant ad - bc is 0, they are parallel (or one is zero), so the image cannot span the plane. Distinct inputs then share an output, and a single-valued inverse mapping back is impossible. Algebraically, solving for x and y returns coefficients divided by ad - bc, so setting it to zero removes exactly the division needed. Note 2x2 matrices only: for larger sizes, ad - bc has no meaning.

blocks.title: Two questions, one order
blocks.body: A cache always asks freshness first. If the stored response is still fresh, it is returned immediately with no network request. Only once the response is stale does the cache consider revalidation with the origin. This ordering is what makes caching fast: most hits never touch the network.

blocks.title: Freshness lifetime
blocks.explanation: Freshness lifetime comes from max-age, or from Expires minus Date for legacy responses. Once age reaches that lifetime the response is stale.

blocks.prompt: Which directive forbids writing the response to any cache at all?

options.label: no-store
no-cache

blocks.rationale: no-store means never persist the response. no-cache still allows storage but forces revalidation before reuse; private restricts storage to the browser; immutable promises the bytes never change, which permits long-lived freshness.

blocks.title: Two separate questions
blocks.body: An HTTP cache first asks: is the stored response still fresh? Freshness is a computed lifetime, so a fresh hit is served with zero network traffic. Only when the response is stale does the cache ask the second question: can I revalidate it cheaply with a conditional request?

blocks.title: Freshness lifetime
blocks.explanation: max-age wins when both are present; otherwise the Expires date minus the Date header is used. The response is fresh while its age is below this lifetime.

blocks.prompt: The stored response is stale, but the server replies 304 Not Modified. What did the cache get?

options.label: A fresh copy of the body from the server
Confirmation to reuse the stored body, refreshed with new metadata
An error, because a stale entry can never be reused

blocks.rationale: 304 carries no body: it means the representation is unchanged, so the stored bytes are reused and their lifetime refreshed. A second max-age can also be sent to extend freshness.

blocks.title: Where this leads
blocks.body: no-store forbids writing anything at all, so it skips this whole pipeline. no-cache does the opposite of what the name suggests: it stores the response but forces revalidation on every use. private restricts storage to the browser only, excluding shared proxies, which matters for per-user responses.

content.title: no-store vs no-cache in one line each
content.body:
no-store: do not put a copy in any cache at all — not in memory, not on disk. Nothing is ever written, so there is nothing to revalidate later.

no-cache: a copy may be stored, but it may not be reused without first checking with the server (revalidation, normally via ETag/If-None-Match). If the server says 304, the stored copy is fine to use.

Mental test: does the response ever end up in the cache? no-store = no. no-cache = yes, but it is rechecked every single time before use.

content.title: Why the names mislead
content.body:
The name no-cache reads as "do not cache", but its real meaning is "do not use a stored copy without revalidating first" — caching is allowed, reuse is not automatic. The name no-store is the one that actually means "do not store".

Also note: no-cache without revalidation machinery still costs a round trip every time; it saves bandwidth (304 body-less replies), not latency. no-store saves neither — it guarantees nothing is retained, which is why it is used for responses containing sensitive or user-specific data that must not be left behind on a shared machine or proxy.

content.title: Why the money problem became a political one
content.body:
The crown's ordinary income could not cover debt service plus spending, and war costs (especially the American war) had made matters worse. Borrowing was not enough, and raising existing taxes on ordinary people was risky and already heavy. The only substantial untapped wealth sat with nobles and clergy, who were largely exempt from the taxes the crown could levy by its own authority.

In the ancien regime, new permanent taxes needed consent from an assembly that represented the kingdom, which is why the Estates-General had to be summoned. Once it met, the disagreement over how it voted (by estate or by head) became inseparable from the tax question: whoever controlled the counting also controlled whether the privileged orders could be taxed.

content.title: Careful with the cause claim
content.body: It is more accurate to say the fiscal crisis made a political confrontation unavoidable than to say it directly created the Revolution. The crown's need for new revenue forced it to convene representatives and bargain over privileges, taxation, and representation. That bargaining quickly exposed the underlying constitutional conflict and made the structure of the Estates-General the central issue.

operations.title: Harmonic Minor: One Change, One Reason

blocks.title: The change
blocks.body: Natural minor becomes harmonic minor by raising scale degree 7 a semitone. Nothing else moves, so the upper half of the scale is what you hear.

blocks.title: Scale degrees
blocks.explanation: Apply flat 3 and flat 6 to a major scale, then raise 7 back to the leading tone. In A: A B C D E F G#.

blocks.title: What the raised 7 buys
blocks.body: Degree 7 now sits a semitone below the tonic, so it pulls upward as a leading tone. The triad on degree 5 also flips from minor to major (in A: E-G#-B), which is the dominant that wants to resolve to i. That pull is the whole motivation for the alteration.

blocks.title: The cost
blocks.body: The gap between flat 6 and 7 becomes three semitones, an augmented second. Melodic minor smooths it by raising 6 too on the way up and reverting to natural minor descending.

blocks.title: Melodic minor as a response to the gap

Minor to major

blocks.rationale: Degree 5 in natural minor is a minor triad; raising degree 7 by a semitone makes its third major, giving the major dominant that resolves strongly to the tonic.

operations.title: Harmonic minor: one alteration, two consequences

blocks.title: The single move
blocks.body: Take natural minor and raise scale degree 7 by one semitone. Everything else stays put. Two things follow directly: degree 7 now sits a semitone below the tonic (a leading note), and the triad rooted on degree 5 becomes major instead of minor.

blocks.title: Scale degrees in A minor
blocks.explanation: Only degree 7 changes: G becomes G sharp, producing a semitone step G sharp to A.

blocks.title: Two consequences
blocks.explanation: The half step creates tonal pull to the tonic, and the major V chord supplies the strong dominant-to-tonic resolution that natural minor lacks.

blocks.title: The price
blocks.body: The raised seventh enlarges the step from degree 6 to degree 7 to three semitones (an augmented second). Melodic minor addresses that gap by also raising degree 6 on the way up, which is why the two forms are taught together.

blocks.prompt: In A harmonic minor, which interval lies between scale degrees 6 and 7?

options.label: Major second (2 semitones)
Minor third (3 semitones)
Augmented second (3 semitones)
Perfect fourth (5 semitones)

blocks.rationale: F to G sharp spans three semitones, the same sound as a minor third but written as a second, since F is the sixth letter name and G sharp the seventh. That augmented second is the characteristic gap of harmonic minor.

content.title: Why raising the sixth removes the gap
content.body: In harmonic minor the step from the lowered sixth to the raised seventh spans three semitones: in A minor, F to G sharp (F-F#-G-G#). Melodic minor raises the sixth to F sharp only while ascending, giving F# to G# — one tone — and the scale runs as a normal stepwise line to the tonic A. Descending, the raised notes are dropped and natural minor returns, so the smooth ascent and the altered dominant chord are both available and the gap never has to be sung.

content.title: Why they are taught as a pair
content.body: Harmonic and melodic minor answer different needs, not different scales-in-themselves. Harmonic minor supplies the raised seventh that makes the V chord major and the leading note strong, and it is the version used for harmony; melodic minor adds the raised sixth so that a melody can climb to that seventh without the three-semitone leap, and it is the version used for stepwise melodic lines. Since both are modifications of the same natural minor, they are learned together rather than as unrelated objects.

blocks.title: The three inputs
blocks.body:
Bayes' rule combines three quantities: the prior P(H), how plausible the hypothesis was before the evidence; the likelihood P(E | H), how well the hypothesis predicts what you actually saw; and the evidence P(E), the total probability of seeing it under all hypotheses. Dropping the prior means reasoning from the likelihood alone, which is the standard error.

The evidence term is a normalizer, not a new ingredient: P(E) = P(E | H)P(H) + P(E | not H)P(not H). It only rescales the two hypotheses so the posterior sums to one.

blocks.title: Bayes' rule
blocks.explanation: Posterior equals likelihood times prior, divided by the total probability of the evidence. The numerator is the joint probability P(E and H).

blocks.title: Why a 99 percent accurate test can mislead
blocks.body:
Take a condition affecting 1 in 10,000 people and a test with 99 percent sensitivity and 99 percent specificity. Among 1,000,000 people, 100 have the condition and about 99 of them test positive. Of the 999,900 healthy people, about 1 percent, roughly 9,999, also test positive. So positives total about 10,098, of which 99 are true: a posterior near 1 percent, not 99 percent.

The test is fine. The huge healthy group generates so many false positives that they swamp the few true positives from the tiny affected group. This is the base rate effect, and it is exactly the prior being ignored.

blocks.title: One million people flow through the test

blocks.rationale: In 1,000 people: 1 has the disease and tests positive; of the 999 healthy, about 5 percent, roughly 50, test positive. So about 1 in 51 positives is a true positive, near 2 percent. The perfect sensitivity does not rescue a small prior.

content.title: Reading the formula

content.title: Why the split matters
content.body: Splitting the reactions between thylakoid membrane and stroma is not just compartment packing. The light reactions pump protons into the thylakoid lumen, so the resulting proton gradient is stored across the thylakoid membrane and drives ATP synthase. The Calvin cycle then runs in the stroma, where ATP and NADPH from the light reactions are available and where the enzymes that fix CO2 work without being exposed to the membrane's electron transport. Keeping them apart lets each set of reactions run under its own conditions instead of competing in one compartment.

operations.title: Action–Reaction Pairs Act on Different Bodies

blocks.title: The key idea
blocks.body: Newton's third law says that if body A exerts a force on body B, then B exerts a force on A that is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. The two forces are always the same type (both gravitational, both contact, etc.) and they never cancel, because each one acts on a different body. A pair of forces can only cancel when they act on the same body.

blocks.title: Third law, symbolically
blocks.explanation: The subscripts name the source and the target. Swapping them and reversing the arrow sign is exactly what the law claims.

blocks.prompt: A book rests on a table. Which pair is a genuine Newton's third law pair?

options.label: The weight of the book and the normal force from the table on the book
The normal force from the table on the book and the push of the book on the table
The weight of the book and the weight of the table

blocks.rationale: Option B is a single interaction between book and table, with each force on a different body, so it is a third law pair. Option A looks balanced only because the book is in equilibrium: those two forces both act on the book, so they can sum to zero but are not a third law pair. Option C mixes two unrelated forces of the same type on different bodies.

blocks.title: Core idea
blocks.body: Osmosis is the net movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane, from a region of higher water potential (lower solute concentration) to a region of lower water potential (higher solute concentration). The membrane lets water through but blocks most solutes, so water moves until the two sides are balanced.

blocks.title: Water potential
blocks.explanation: Total water potential (\Psi) is the sum of solute potential (\Psi_s, usually negative) and pressure potential (\Psi_p). Pure water at atmospheric pressure has \Psi = 0. Water always moves down a \Psi gradient, toward the lower (more negative) value. Adding solute lowers \Psi_s, which is why water moves toward the more concentrated solution.

blocks.prompt: Two solutions are separated by a selectively permeable membrane. Solution A has a higher solute concentration than solution B. Which way does water move net?

options.label: From A to B
From B to A
No net movement

blocks.rationale: B has more water (higher water potential) and A has more solute (lower water potential), so water moves down the water-potential gradient from B to A.

results.note: Almost nothing to explain, so overlap scores are meaningless here and only validity matters.

content.title: Osmosis: the deeper picture
content.body: "Water moves" is only half the story. Osmosis is the net diffusion of water across a semipermeable membrane from the side with higher water concentration (lower solute concentration) to the side with lower water concentration (higher solute concentration). The membrane blocks solutes but lets water pass, so water itself is the moving particle. "Net" matters: water crosses both ways, but the overall flow goes toward the more concentrated solution. It needs no energy input; it is passive. Two commonly confused points: (1) it is the water that moves, not the solute seeking balance, and (2) osmosis stops (or slows) only when the osmotic pressure opposing the flow balances it, not simply when concentrations are equal in every setup.

content.title: Osmotic pressure, in one line
content.body: Osmotic pressure is the pressure that must be applied to the more concentrated side to stop net water movement. For dilute solutions it scales with solute concentration and temperature, roughly pi = i M R T, where M is molarity, R the gas constant, T the absolute temperature, and i the number of particles a solute dissociates into (for example, i = 2 for NaCl). This is why ionic solutes exert more osmotic pressure than the same molar amount of a non-dissociating solute such as glucose.

content.title: Correction: seasons are not caused by distance
content.body: The note is wrong on both counts. Distance is not the cause of seasons: Earth's orbit is nearly circular, and in fact the northern hemisphere's winter (early January) occurs near perihelion, the closest point to the Sun. Seasons come from Earth's axial tilt (~23.4 degrees). Whichever hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun receives sunlight at a steeper angle and for more hours per day, so it is warmer. The hemispheres are therefore in opposite seasons at the same time, not the same season.

content.title: Why tilt matters
content.body: Two effects combine: higher Sun angle concentrates the same solar energy on a smaller area, and longer days give more total heating time. At the equinoxes the tilt is sideways to the Sun, so both hemispheres get roughly equal daylight.

content.rationale: Seasons are caused by the tilt of Earth's axis (about 23.5 degrees), not by distance from the Sun. The tilt makes sunlight strike each hemisphere more directly and for longer days during its summer. Because the hemispheres point opposite ways along the orbit, they experience opposite seasons at the same time. Earth's orbit is slightly elliptical, but that variation is too small and does not match the timing of the seasons.

operations.title: The Simple Pendulum: Period and Amplitude

blocks.title: What the log is actually claiming
blocks.body: The log repeats one and the same result 33 times: releasing from the same marked angle and timing twenty swings gives a period that varies by less than the reading error. Repetition is not 33 independent tests — it is one measurement protocol restated. The justified conclusion is narrow: for the angles used, the period is independent of amplitude to within the stated uncertainty. This is the small-angle (isochronism) regime, not a general law.

blocks.title: Period of a simple pendulum
blocks.explanation: L is the pendulum length, g the local gravitational field strength, and theta_0 the release amplitude in radians. The leading term 2*pi*sqrt(L/g) is independent of amplitude; the correction grows only quadratically in theta_0, so it is negligible when theta_0 is small. This explains why the log saw no detectable change.

blocks.title: How sensitive is the correction?
blocks.body: The fractional shift in period is about theta_0^2/16. At theta_0 = 0.1 rad (about 5.7 degrees) that is roughly 6e-4, i.e. 0.06 percent — below a typical stopwatch reading error. At theta_0 = 0.5 rad (about 29 degrees) it is about 1.6 percent, which a twenty-swing timing would easily resolve. So the log's null result is expected at small angles and would not survive at large ones.

blocks.prompt: A pendulum is timed at theta_0 = 0.05 rad, then at theta_0 = 0.05 rad again with a different student timing. The period agrees within reading error. What is the best-supported conclusion?

options.label: The period is exactly independent of amplitude at all amplitudes.
For small amplitudes, the period is independent of amplitude to within the measurement uncertainty.
The period depends on who does the timing.
The period depends strongly on amplitude.

blocks.rationale: The measurement only probes small amplitudes and is limited by reading error, so it supports the small-angle isochronism claim, not an exact or all-amplitude one. The quadratic correction is far too small to detect here.

content.title: These 33 observations are one observation
content.body: Every entry repeats the same procedure and result word for word: same release angle, twenty swings, period change below the reading error. Repeating an identical trial is not independent evidence, so this log supports the claim at most once, not 33 times. Checking repeatability is useful, but only varied amplitudes (experimental groups) count as separate tests of the amplitude claim.

content.title: What the result actually shows
content.body: The small-angle period is T \approx 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}, independent of amplitude. That independence only holds for small angles; the exact period grows with amplitude, roughly as T \approx T_0 (1 + \theta_0^2/16) for amplitude \theta_0 in radians. So a constant angle cannot test amplitude dependence at all, and the claim would fail at large release angles. Note the wording: period over twenty swings divided by 20 is the period, so timing many swings only reduces timing error, it does not remove same-angle sampling error.
